name: What drove the late-medieval transition: population or class power?

positions.claim: Population pressing against land drove the medieval cycle: growth to 1300, crisis, plague, recovery.
positions.mech: Rising numbers cut holdings and wages and raised rents; plague reversed every ratio.
for: English wages, rents and land values move as the model predicts after 1348 (Postan, Hatcher).
Languedoc shows the same rise-and-fall cycle in tithes and land registers 1500-1700 (Le Roy Ladurie).
against: The same plague produced freedom in England and serfdom in Poland, which the population model cannot explain (Brenner).

positions.claim: Identical demographic shocks had opposite outcomes because the balance of class power differed: what mattered was who won the struggle over surplus.
positions.mech: In England lords lost serfdom but kept land and leased it to capitalist tenants; in France peasants kept land; in the east lords re-enserfed.
for: Divergent outcomes of the same plague in England, France and eastern Europe.
English leasehold farms show rising productivity by 1700.
against: Too little weight on markets and towns; English peasants were often already market-dependent before 1500 (Hatcher & Bailey).
Comparative cases were chosen to fit; Dutch and Flemish growth came from smallholders.

positions.claim: Feudalism had an internal tendency to crisis: the per-head levy fell as holdings shrank, pushing lords toward war and coercion.
positions.mech: Falling seigneurial income led to war and fiscal states; peasant resistance (1381) set the limits.
for: Eastern Normandy's seigneurial revenues fall from c.1315, before the plague (Bois).
Revolts of 1358, 1378 and 1381 follow labour laws and war taxes.
against: Hard to separate the "falling levy" from plain Malthusian decline.

positions.claim: Scarce labour can mean freedom or bondage; which one depends on whether lords can coordinate to stop peasants moving.
positions.mech: Where states and diets let lords enforce bondage they did; where competition among lords for tenants won, wages and freedom rose.
for: English serfdom faded by negotiation within two generations (Bailey).
Domar's model fits Russia and the Baltic.
against: Says what is possible, not which outcome happens.

state: Few now hold either pure position. The working consensus combines the plague shock with institutions: who could move, who controlled land, and whether towns and states backed lords or tenants.
settle: Manor-level series of rents, wages, tenure types and mobility for England, France and Poland on a common basis, to test whether outcomes followed class institutions or prices.
fun: The same plague freed English serfs and chained Polish ones: was it the rats or the lords?

name: Did the Black Death set Europe on the road to the Great Divergence?

positions.claim: The plague raised incomes per head and Europe's lethal cities and wars kept them high, while late marriage restrained births.
positions.mech: Higher incomes fed urban demand; urban death and war held population down; pastoral farming delayed marriage.
for: Urbanisation and wages in western Europe stay above pre-plague levels for centuries.
Fertility restriction tracks pastoral shares.
against: Wages in most of Europe fell back by 1600 (Allen, Clark).
Humphries & Weisdorf find annual incomes, not day wages, rose less.

positions.claim: The shock was common; institutions decided whether gains lasted. North Sea towns and parliaments kept them; Mamluk Egypt's absentee lords lost them.
positions.mech: Strong representative and urban institutions resisted lords' attempts to claw back wages and rents.
for: Egypt's output fell for 150 years after the same mortality that freed English labour (Borsch).
Wage gains survived only in England and the Low Countries (Pamuk).
against: Institutions themselves may be products of earlier commercial geography.

positions.claim: Late marriage and female wage labour, strengthened after the plague, broke the Malthusian link in north-western Europe.
positions.mech: Fewer births per woman and more human capital let incomes stay above subsistence.
for: North Sea women married in their mid-twenties and worked as servants.
against: The pattern was strongest in slow-growing Germany and Scandinavia (Dennison & Ogilvie).

positions.claim: The post-plague boom was a Malthusian windfall that faded as population recovered; the divergence came later and for other reasons.
positions.mech: Real wages track population inversely until c.1800.
for: English real wages fell back to around pre-plague levels by 1600.
Wage series that ignore days worked overstate post-plague gains (Humphries & Weisdorf).
against: London and Amsterdam held their gains, which needs explaining.

positions.claim: The plague broke a Eurasian trade system centred on Asia and the Islamic world; Europe later rose into the vacuum.
positions.mech: Disruption of overland and Indian Ocean circuits after 1350 weakened the old cores more than peripheral Europe.
for: Trade through Baghdad, Cairo and the steppe routes shrank after 1350.
against: Europe's own trade shrank too; the gap opened only after 1500.

state: Most economic historians now accept that the plague mattered for the "little divergence" within Europe, but disagree on whether through demography, institutions or both; the synthesis by Jedwab, Johnson and Koyama stresses that effects differed by place.
settle: Comparable wage, urban and fertility series for Egypt, Anatolia, Italy and the North Sea from 1300 to 1600, with plague mortality estimated locally.
fun: Half of Europe died, and the survivors got a pay rise: but why did it stick in London and not in Cairo?

name: Did Islam end the ancient Mediterranean economy and make Charlemagne possible?

positions.claim: Roman Mediterranean unity survived the Germanic invasions and was broken only by the Arab conquests; the West turned inland and Carolingian Europe was born.
positions.mech: Loss of eastern imports (papyrus, spices, gold) after c.650-700 cut Gaul off.
for: Papyrus and eastern spices vanish from Frankish documents in the late 7th century.
against: Archaeology shows decline well before 650 (Hodges & Whitehouse; Wickham).
Arab conquerors traded readily with Christians (Dennett; Lopez).

positions.claim: The Mediterranean economy collapsed in the 6th century; the Carolingian revival was northern, fed by Abbasid silver via the Baltic.
positions.mech: Silver dirhams through Russia and Scandinavia stimulated North Sea emporia.
for: Mediterranean amphorae and shipwrecks drop sharply after c.550.
Huge dirham hoards in Gotland and Sweden.
against: Northern silver mostly arrives after 800, late for the first revival.

positions.claim: Communications revived from c.775; Europeans paid for Muslim silver and luxuries chiefly by selling captives.
positions.mech: Venice and Frankish traders exported slaves to the caliphate, bringing coin back west.
for: Hundreds of recorded voyages and travellers 700-900.
Dirham and dinar finds in the Frankish world and the slave markets of Venice.
against: Volume of the slave trade is hard to measure.

positions.claim: Exchange shrank because the Roman fiscal state that moved goods dissolved; regional aristocracies then set the scale of trade.
positions.mech: When the tax-and-army system ended, bulk shipping lost its main customer.
for: Regional pottery networks shrink in step with state collapse.
against: Underplays long-distance links that survived.

positions.claim: Arabs had no policy of blockade; changes in trade had many causes, and Islamic gold and silver later helped the West.
positions.mech: Commercial patterns shifted with taste and coinage, not religious war.
for: Christian-Muslim trade continued in the 8th-10th centuries.
against: Written before most of the archaeology.

state: Pirenne's question still frames the field, but his answer does not: the decline started earlier and the revival had Islamic money behind it, as ice cores tracking Frankish silver mining now help to date.
settle: More dated shipwrecks, coin finds and ice-core lead series that pin down when exchange fell and when it revived.
fun: Without Muhammad, no Charlemagne, said Pirenne; the shipwrecks say the sea was empty before the Arabs came.

name: Was there such a thing as feudalism?

positions.claim: Feudalism names a real social order: bonds of vassalage and fiefs among warriors, lordship over peasants, fragmented public power.
positions.mech: After the Carolingian collapse, protection and land were exchanged for service.
for: Rich vocabulary of homage, fidelity and fief in 11th-12th century sources.
against: Built on later legal texts read back into earlier centuries (Reynolds).

positions.claim: "Feudalism" is a modern abstraction that distorts the evidence; fiefs and vassalage as a system were invented by 12th-13th century lawyers.
positions.mech: Property and political obligations were more varied, and collective, than the model allows.
for: Few early sources use "fief" in the textbook sense (Reynolds).
against: Historians still need a word for lordship-based societies.

positions.claim: Public order collapsed abruptly around 1000, replaced by castellan lordship and new exactions.
positions.mech: Castles and mounted retinues let local lords seize justice and impose "bad customs".
for: Mâconnais charters show public courts vanishing c.980-1030 (Duby).
against: The change is in the documents, not society (Barthélemy, White).

positions.claim: Continuity: lordship and violence were old; the "revolution" reflects changing records.
positions.mech: Charters replaced court notices, making old practice visible.
for: Pre-1000 sources already show lords coercing peasants.
against: Some breaks, like castle building, are real and dated.

positions.claim: Use "feudal" for a way of taking surplus from peasants and compare it worldwide: Europe's version, with lords who could bargain with kings, differs from tributary China or Islamic states that used slave soldiers.
positions.mech: Decentralised military lordship constrained rulers and produced parliaments.
for: European rulers' reigns lengthen after c.1000 relative to sultans (Blaydes & Chaney).
Parliaments spread across Latin Europe after 1188.
against: Stretching the term worldwide may empty it.

state: Most medievalists avoid "feudalism" as a system and talk of lordship; comparativists and economists still use it, now mostly to ask why Latin Europe's fragmented power produced constraints on rulers.
settle: Systematic comparison of charters and court records across regions before and after 1000, and of rulers' tenure and assemblies across Eurasia.
fun: Ask ten historians to define feudalism and you get eleven answers, which is why some want to ban the word.

name: What caused the Great Famine of 1315-17, and did it prepare the Black Death?

positions.claim: The end of the medieval climate regime brought years of torrential rain; harvests failed regardless of population.
positions.mech: Cold, wet seasons rotted grain and drowned pastures; a cattle plague followed.
for: Chroniclers across northern Europe record continuous rain in 1315-16.
Tree rings and grain yields fall together.
against: Similar weather in earlier centuries did not kill on this scale.

positions.claim: An overpopulated countryside on poor soils had no reserves; the rain only triggered a crisis long in the making.
positions.mech: Smallholders with too little land could not survive a run of bad harvests.
for: Deaths concentrated among the land-poor (Kershaw).
Rents and land prices peaked c.1300.
against: Population growth had slowed by 1300 in many places.

positions.claim: War, purveyance and hoarding made bad harvests into famine; institutions failed to move grain.
positions.mech: Scottish raids, Flemish wars and royal requisitions took the reserves.
for: Northern England and Flanders, both war zones, suffered worst.
against: Hard to separate from the weather everywhere else.

positions.claim: Survivors of the famine and the loss of milk cows grew into frailer adults who died more readily of plague in 1348.
positions.mech: Childhood malnutrition weakened later immunity.
for: London skeletons show frailty markers predicted Black Death deaths.
against: Plague killed healthy and frail alike in many places.

state: Campbell's climate-and-disease synthesis is dominant, but most accept that overpopulation and war set the scale of the dying.
settle: Finer dating of the 1310s climate shift, more skeletal samples from famine and plague cemeteries, and manorial yields set against local population density.
fun: Three wet summers, a cattle plague and a famine that may have made the Black Death worse: the 14th century's warm-up act.

name: Did the printing press make the Reformation?

positions.claim: Print transformed European culture by fixing, standardising and multiplying texts; without it Luther would have been another Hus.
positions.mech: Identical copies spread faster than suppression could act.
for: Luther's tracts reached all German lands within weeks.
against: Overstates fixity; early print was full of error and piracy (Johns).

positions.claim: Luther and Wittenberg's printers built a new genre, the short vernacular pamphlet, and that turned a dispute into a movement.
positions.mech: Cheap, quick, branded tracts in German.
for: Luther became the most-printed author of his age within a few years.
against: Most people heard rather than read the message.

positions.claim: Towns with early presses were likelier to turn Protestant and grew faster.
positions.mech: Print lowered the cost of spreading ideas and business knowledge.
for: Instrumenting with distance from Mainz keeps the effect (Rubin; Dittmar).
against: Measures adoption, not belief; towns may have differed in unmeasured ways.

positions.claim: In a largely illiterate society, the Reformation spread by sermon, song and woodcut; print was one channel among many.
positions.mech: Literate readers relayed print to listeners; communal politics decided adoption.
for: Woodcut propaganda and sermons reached villages that bought no books.
against: The woodcuts were printed too.

positions.claim: The Ottoman world delayed Muslim printing because rulers relied on clerical legitimacy and learning travelled person to person; Europe's fragmented authority could not stop the press.
positions.mech: Print threatened religious gatekeepers whom sultans needed.
for: Arabic-script printing for Muslims waited until 1727 in Istanbul.
against: The famous 1485 ban is poorly documented; demand and the cost of reproducing calligraphy mattered too.

state: Few doubt print mattered; the argument is now over mechanism (pamphlets, literacy, markets) and why the same technology had different effects in China, the Ottoman world and Europe.
settle: Town-level data on presses, pamphlet editions, literacy and confessional choice, and comparative work on demand for print outside Europe.
fun: Luther posted 95 theses; his printers posted his face on half of Germany.

name: Was there a military revolution, and did it make Europe conquer the world?

positions.claim: Dutch and Swedish drill and linear tactics required permanent armies, which built states.
positions.mech: Drilled musketry needed trained, paid soldiers year-round.
for: Standing armies appear in the Netherlands and Sweden.
against: The changes were older and came in bursts (Rogers), or later (Black).

positions.school: Fortress revolution and the rise of the West
positions.claim: Artillery forts forced bigger armies, navies and taxes from 1500 to 1800, and gave Europeans the edge to claim a third of the globe.
positions.mech: Bastions, gunned ships and drilled infantry.
for: European claims rose to about 35 percent of world land by 1800.
against: Asian and Ottoman armies kept pace for long periods (Andrade, Ágoston).

positions.claim: Revolutions came earlier and in bursts, in the Hundred Years' War infantry and artillery revolutions.
positions.mech: Sharp changes then long adaptation.
for: Crécy and the French siege train of the 1440s-50s.
against: Blurs a single revolution into many changes.

positions.claim: The big growth came after 1660 and owed more to state-elite cooperation than to technology.
positions.mech: Absolutist bargains financed armies.
for: Army sizes peak under Louis XIV.
against: Downplays 16th-century change.

positions.claim: Hoffman: constant competitive war with cheap capital pushed Europe ahead in gunpowder technology. Andrade and Sharman: the gap opened late, and early expansion owed more to disease, allies and Asian indifference.
positions.mech: Learning by fighting versus contingent advantages.
for: Price of gunpowder weapons fell fastest in Europe (Hoffman).
Ming and Qing victories over Europeans; European dependence on local rulers in Asia and Africa.
against: Each side finds it hard to explain the other's evidence.

state: Most accept major military change with large fiscal consequences; dating and the link to global conquest are disputed, and the global turn (Andrade, Sharman) has weakened claims of an early European edge.
settle: Comparable data on army sizes, weapons prices and battle outcomes across Europe, the Ottoman empire, Mughal India, China and Africa.
fun: Bastions, drill and debt: did Europe out-fight the world, or just out-borrow it?

name: Was there a general crisis in the 17th century, and did the climate cause it?

positions.claim: The last crisis of the feudal economy cleared the way for capitalism in England and the Netherlands.
positions.mech: Markets were too narrow; crisis concentrated capital.
for: Mediterranean and central Europe stagnated while the North Sea grew.
against: Crisis was not general in economic terms (de Vries).

positions.claim: Swollen courts and offices drained the country, and the 1640s revolts were the reaction.
positions.mech: Costly Renaissance states lost legitimacy.
for: Simultaneous revolts in England, France, Spain's realms.
against: Does not fit the Ottoman or Chinese crises.

positions.claim: The Little Ice Age, at its worst in the mid-century, brought harvest failures that pushed overstretched states into revolt and war worldwide.
positions.mech: Cold and drought cut harvests while war and taxes rose: a fatal synergy.
for: Revolts cluster in the coldest decades from England to China.
Celali revolts follow the coldest years in Anatolia.
against: Temperature records do not show a sustained European shift (Kelly & Ó Gráda).
Cold periods were not synchronous worldwide (Neukom).

positions.claim: Population recovery since 1450 overloaded states and elites; bad harvests struck societies already near breaking.
positions.mech: Prices, elite overproduction and fiscal strain.
for: Revolts follow population peaks in England, France, China and the Ottoman lands.
against: Plays down climate and war.

positions.claim: The economic crisis was regional: the Dutch thrived in the cold, and climate effects are easily overstated.
positions.mech: Adaptive commercial societies turned shocks to advantage.
for: Dutch shipping and finance grew through the coldest decades.
against: Dutch success may be the exception that proves the rule.

state: Parker's Global Crisis has made climate central, but most specialists treat it as one stress among war, debt and population, and stress that some societies did well.
settle: Annually resolved regional climate reconstructions matched with harvest, price and revolt data across Eurasia.
fun: The sun went quiet, the harvests failed, kings lost their heads, and Hobbes wrote Leviathan.

name: What caused the 16th-century price revolution?

positions.claim: American silver raised Europe's money supply and so its prices.
positions.mech: Quantity theory: more silver, higher prices.
for: Treasure arrivals at Seville and Spanish prices rise together to the 1590s.
against: Inflation started before American silver (Nef, Fischer); English prices tracked grain more than silver (Goldstone).

positions.claim: Population growth and urbanisation drove up food prices and the velocity of money.
positions.mech: Demand outran supply of food; town trade sped up circulation.
for: Grain prices rose much faster than manufactures.
against: Hard to get sustained inflation without more money.

positions.claim: Price revolutions are demand-driven waves that end in crisis.
positions.mech: Population and expectations, with money following.
for: Similar waves in the 13th, 16th, 18th and 20th centuries.
against: Waves are hard to test.

positions.claim: China's demand for silver priced the world's silver; Europe's inflation ended when silver's value fell to China's level.
positions.mech: Arbitrage from Potosí and Japan to China via Manila and the Indian Ocean.
for: Silver was worth about twice as much in China around 1600.
against: Chinese demand cannot explain the timing of early European inflation.

positions.claim: Barkan: European silver brought inflation to the Ottomans. Pamuk: the main cause was the state's own debasement under war pressure.
positions.mech: Silver inflow versus coin debasement.
for: Ottoman prices jump with the 1585-86 debasement.
against: Barkan's price data were thin.

state: Monetary and demographic causes are now combined; the global silver story has pushed the debate beyond Europe.
settle: Better mint and money-stock series and regional price series across Europe, the Ottoman empire and China.
fun: Silver dug in the Andes paid Chinese taxes and raised the price of bread in Seville.

name: What made north-western Europe rich before industry: Atlantic trade, slavery or harder work?

positions.claim: Atlantic trade enriched merchants in already-constrained monarchies, who won stronger property rights; growth followed.
positions.mech: Trade profits shift power to merchants, who reshape institutions.
for: Growth concentrated in Atlantic nations and ports.
against: Spain and Portugal traded most but did not grow.
Trade volumes small until 1800 (O'Rourke & Williamson).

positions.claim: The slave trade and plantation economy financed and demanded British industry.
positions.mech: Profits and Atlantic markets for manufactures.
for: West African and Caribbean markets took much of Britain's export growth.
against: Profits were small relative to investment (O'Brien, Eltis & Engerman).

positions.claim: The periphery was peripheral; Europe's growth came from its own markets.
positions.mech: Domestic demand and investment dominated.
for: Colonial trade profits under a few percent of investment.
against: Ignores linkages and the ghost acres.

positions.claim: Households chose to work longer and more for the market to buy new goods, raising output before machines; Japan had its own version.
positions.mech: Consumer desire reallocates household time.
for: Longer work years in England (Voth); Dutch market consumption.
Japanese peasants substituted labour for animals (Hayami).
against: Many worked longer because they were poorer (Allen & Weisdorf); institutions blocked it in Germany (Ogilvie).

positions.claim: Europe and advanced Asia were similar until c.1750; Britain broke out with coal, New World land and the challenge of Indian textiles; high wages made machines pay.
positions.mech: Ecological relief and factor prices, not culture.
for: Yangzi delta living standards close to England's c.1750 (Pomeranz).
British cotton imitated Indian calico (Parthasarathi).
against: Wage data show an earlier gap (Broadberry & Gupta).

state: Few accept a single cause. Atlantic institutions, coal and high wages, and the industrious household are often combined; the timing of the gap with Asia is the main live dispute.
settle: Comparable real-income and hours-of-work series across Europe and Asia, and better estimates of colonial profits and linkages.
fun: Sugar in your tea made you work harder: or did the slaves who grew it make Britain rich?
